newsitem.title: UK: Britain plugs tax loophole on share buybacks.
newsitem.headline: Britain plugs tax loophole on share buybacks.

text.p: Britain took stock markets and investors by surprise Tuesday with an announcement that it was plugging a tax loophole that has allowed a growing number of companies to enrich investors through stock buybacks.

In a move that will save the government up to 400 million British pounds ($625 million) a year, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke announced that shareholders would no longer be able to claim tax credits on share buybacks or special dividend payouts, effective immediately.
The London stock market suffered a sharp dive immediately after the government announcement, but by afternoon it had returned to positive ground.
Dealers said the initial reaction to the tax ruling had been exaggerated. They said that while the timing of the announcement had been a surprise, its content was not.
The decision was expected to impact British companies that so far this year have announced plans to spend up to 2.5 billion pounds ($4 billion) buying back their own shares.

Reuters Holdings Plc, the global news and information organisation, responded to the announcement by postponing shareholder consideration of its plan to return 613 million pounds ($958 million) to shareholders through a stock buyback and special dividend.

A Reuters shareholders meeting had been scheduled for Wednesday to approve the proposal. A source close to Treasury officials said that they were "... well aware of this date" when deciding on the timing of Tuesday's announcement.
"A decision after that date would clearly have been more difficult for the company," the source said.
"The timing is no coincidence ... It's crystal clear that it's aimed at Reuters special dividend shares," said Roger Muray, a tax partner at accountants Ernst & Young.
In Britain, share buybacks are most beneficial to tax-exempt shareholders, principally pension funds, which can claim tax credits from the government.

"We have seen recently companies buying their own shares or paying special dividends in such a way that the proceeds end up almost entirely in the hands of those who are entitled to payment of a tax credit," Clarke said.
"This has costs for the Exchequer (Treasury) and, if action is not taken soon, that cost would escalate," Clarke said in announcing the new ruling.

"The government takes a firm attitude on tax avoidance ... the scale of the exploitation means it had reached a point where the Chancellor had to act because of the costs involved," said a spokeswoman for the tax authorities.

The Treasury's Financial Secretary, Michael Jack, said the cost of companies taking advantage of tax credits on share buybacks had risen to an unacceptable level and the government had been considering tax changes since last year.
"Then the number of people using this scheme was very much at the level of the trickle, but the trickle has turned into something of a river," Jack said.
Shares in a string of top British companies planning buybacks, including several banks and utilities, fell amid concerns that the ruling makes the plans less attractive to their major investors.

Reuters ended the day down 20.5 pence at 756.5 pence on the London Stock Exchange, after earlier hitting a low of 750. In the United States, American Depositary Receipts of Reuters fell $2.25 to $70.875 on the Nasdaq market.

The ruling removes some of the tax advantages that had applied to pension funds. The funds are exempt from tax, enabling them to reclaim the 25 percent advance corporation tax paid by companies on dividends.

Clarke said pension funds could no longer claim tax credit payments -- which currently mean that a one pound net dividend is worth 1.25 pounds to a pension fund -- on buybacks or on some special dividends.
Experts said the biggest implication of Clarke's measure was for share buybacks.

These were particularly lucrative for pension funds, which were able to treat the difference between the buyback price and the price at which the stock was originally issued as a dividend "distribution" payment on which they could reclaim the 25 percent tax.
Still, experts said, companies generating cash surpluses were unlikely to abandon the objective of returning some of that cash to shareholders in the most tax efficient way possible.

"There is no secret a lot of companies have surplus cash," said Terry Awan, senior tax partner at Arthur Andersen. "This is a fairly significant move that means companies will have to think of other ways to create incentives for shareholders."
